title: A Legacy of Innovation: 125 Years on the Camden Waterfront
summary: 125 years. One community. A legacy that put voices on the moon and keeps warfighters connected today.
body_markdown:
There are not many places in America where you can stand in a single spot and trace more than a century of culturally impactful technological history beneath your feet. Camden, New Jersey is one of them.


What began in 1901 as a small machine shop where an ambitious inventor with a simple belief that recorded sound could be improved has, over 125 years and through remarkable transformation, grown into one of the nation's most consequential centers of defense and communications innovation. The names above the door have changed many times over. The spirit inside has not.


**Victor Talking Machine Company, Camden, NJ Incorporated October 3, 1901 with Eldridge Reeves Johnson as President**


Victor Talking Machine Company, Camden, NJ Incorporated Octo...


Eldridge Johnson incorporated the Victor Talking Machine Co. in Camden at the turn of the 20th century, and what followed was far greater than anyone could have anticipated. Victor didn't simply manufacture products. It helped transform how the world experienced music and information, and in doing so, helped establish Camden as a place where ambitious ideas became reality. The iconic image of Nipper the dog listening to “His Master's Voice” became one of the most recognized symbols in the world, and it was born in Camden.


When the Radio Corporation of America acquired Victor in 1929, it brought together two pioneering legacies and launched a new chapter of innovation from the same Camden address. The following decades saw the workforce contribute to some of the defining technological achievements of the 20th century: radio, television, radar and advanced communications. Each new frontier brought new challenges, and each time, the people of Camden rose to the occasion.


Perhaps nothing captures that spirit more vividly than what happened in the summer of 1969. When Neil Armstrong and Buzz Aldrin became the first humans to set foot on the moon’s surface, they used technology developed in Camden to transmit their voices back to Earth. It is the kind of fact that deserves a moment of quiet reflection. People working in Camden helped make possible one of the most extraordinary moments in human history.


That legacy surged beyond the space race through many corporate chapters, including General Electric, Lockheed Martin and the heritage companies in between. In 2019, two pioneering organizations came together to form L3Harris, fortified by a team well-versed in delivering technology to solve some of the world's most complex challenges.


PHOTO CREDIT: NASA | CAMDEN, N.J. – RCA Camden played a major role in some of NASA's most critical programs. When Neil Armstrong and Edward "Buzz" Aldrin, Jr., became the first human beings to set foot on the moon in 1969, they communicated with each other as well as the rest of the world through backpack radio systems built at RCA's Camden facility.

What has remained constant, across every era and every transition, is the character of the workforce itself: the engineers who refused to accept that something couldn't be done; the machinists and technicians who turned ideas into hardware; and the scientists who kept asking harder questions. Generation after generation of Camden employees have maintained the same fundamental conviction: that whatever exists today could be made better tomorrow.


That conviction is as alive today as it has ever been. The work happening in Camden right now is as important and consequential as anything the site has ever produced. L3Harris employees are developing, building and delivering some of the most advanced communications and defense technologies in the world. These technologies include anti-jam communication systems that keep warfighters connected when adversaries are doing everything in their power to cut them off; resilient command, control and communications networks that allow U.S. forces to operate across ships, submarines, aircraft and shore sites in the most contested environments imaginable; and the next generation of encryption and cybersecurity capabilities that protect the nation's most sensitive networks, platforms and missions.


The stakes of that work are not abstract. Somewhere right now, a sailor is operating in contested waters, a pilot is depending on their communications technologies to keep them connected and a commander is relying on a secure network to make decisions that matter. The systems those warfighters depend on were built and tested in Camden.


What makes this 125-year milestone meaningful is not the number itself. It is the unbroken thread of ingenuity and commitment that connects Eldridge Johnson's machine shop to the advanced defense technologies being developed in Camden today. It is the generations of employees who applied their creativity and expertise to support their customers' vital missions. It is also the current workforce, carrying that legacy forward into a technological landscape that would be unrecognizable to the company's founders, but driven by the same belief that has always defined Camden.


The future, as the Camden team has proven time and again, does not simply arrive. It is imagined, designed, built and delivered by people who believe that what is possible today is only the beginning of what comes next. For 125 years, that has been the story of Camden. And by every measure, the most important chapters are still being written.
